title: Piano Concerto No. 2, Adagio: Rachmaninoff and Richter
work: Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 18 — II. Adagio sostenuto, opening-side comparison only
question: How do Rachmaninoff and Richter keep the Adagio’s melody continuous as it passes from flute and clarinet to piano?
intro: Muted strings make the short modulation from C minor to E major, and the piano enters quietly with a repeated figure. Flute and clarinet play a melody that the piano later takes over. Rachmaninoff and Stokowski recorded these opening phrases in Philadelphia in 1929; Richter and Wisłocki recorded them with the Warsaw Philharmonic in 1959.

recordings.label: Rachmaninoff, Stokowski, Philadelphia Orchestra, 1929
recordings.note: The composer played at Philadelphia’s Academy of Music on 10 April 1929; this opening side preserves the first take of the passage.

recordings.label: Richter, Wisłocki, Warsaw Philharmonic, 1959
recordings.note: The Warsaw Philharmonic accompanies Richter in the 1959 Deutsche Grammophon recording of the complete concerto.

passages.label: Broken-chord figures in E major
passages.note: The strings move to E major, and the piano plays the chord as quiet, repeated broken-chord figures. The wind melody enters later.

passages.label: Clarinet melody over piano arpeggios
passages.note: The clarinet plays the long melody over even arpeggios in the piano; the strings hold the harmony beneath them.

passages.label: Melody in the piano
passages.note: The piano now plays the melody in its upper notes, while the clarinet plays quick figures around it.
